extractedText: Opinion Long read · 12 min “ SoftBank's Arm and OpenAI Bet Is Vision Fund 3 in Everything but Name SoftBank's 2024 to 2026 capital deployment looks like a series of opportunistic AI bets. Read together, the OpenAI follow-on, the Stargate equity slot, the Ampere and ABB acquisitions, the Nvidia exit, and the 20-billion-dollar margin facility against Arm shares add up to one thing: a third Vision Fund being financed off the SoftBank Group balance sheet because the Gulf-LP base for a marketed vehicle no longer exists at the required scale. Adrian Watkins Founder 30 May 2026 Key takeaways SoftBank's 2024 to 2026 capital rotation looks like a series of opportunistic AI bets, but the structure (Arm balance-sheet leverage, Stargate equity, OpenAI follow-on, Ampere absorption into the AI Computing Segment) is a single thesis that adds up to Vision Fund 3 without the marketing. SoftBank's published loan-to-value ratio climbed sharply across the second half of 2025 and another step up is implied after the late-March 2026 unsecured bridge facility; this is the unmistakable signature of a third Vision Fund being financed off the balance sheet rather than off LP capital. Saudi PIF, which underwrote roughly 45 per cent of the original Vision Fund, was not anchored into Vision Fund 2 and is structurally unlikely to anchor a Vision Fund 3 in the open market while it is funding HUMAIN at home; that absence is the reason the marketing has not happened, not a reason the thesis is missing. Arm's role has quietly shifted from architecture licensor to financing engine: the syndicated margin facility against Arm shares (about USD 8.5 billion drawn against a much larger ceiling) and SoftBank's controlling Arm ownership together underwrite the next OpenAI tranche if Stargate equity calls land before Arm's CSS and AI Computing Segment revenues compound. For non-Japanese investors, the cleanest TSE-listed expression of this thesis is 9984.T itself (ADR ticker SFTBY); buying Arm separately is a smaller, cleaner bet on the same compounding royalty stream but does not capture the OpenAI 11 per cent stake or the Stargate equity, which only sit on the SoftBank Group balance sheet. SoftBank's 2024 to 2026 capital deployment has rotated decisively. The pieces are individually familiar. An Arm follow-on listing that did not happen but was prepared. A leading equity slot inside the Stargate consortium with OpenAI, Oracle and MGX. A USD 30 billion follow-on into OpenAI on top of the prior tranche, financed by a forty-billion-dollar unsecured bridge in late March 2026. A clean exit from the Nvidia common-stock position at USD 5.83 billion. A trimmed T-Mobile position. The acquisition of Ampere Computing for USD 6.5 billion and ABB's robotics arm for USD 5.375 billion, both folded into a new "AI Computing Segment" alongside Arm and Graphcore. Read separately, each looks like an opportunistic bet by an investor with conviction about where compute is going. Read together, they are the third Vision Fund in everything but the marketing. The reason the marketing has not happened is not strategic ambiguity. It is the very specific fact that Saudi PIF, which anchored the first Vision Fund in 2017 and declined to underwrite Vision Fund 2 in any comparable scale, is now spending its sovereign AI capital domestically through HUMAIN. With the largest available anchor LP unwilling and the second-largest, Mubadala, focused on its own G42 and AIQ commitments, a public fundraise of the kind the original Vision Fund ran would not clear at a credible cover ratio. So Masayoshi Son is doing the next-best thing. He is financing Vision Fund 3 off the SoftBank Group balance sheet, with Arm as the load-bearing collateral, and is letting the public narrative call it a series of one-off bets.
